'Zubin, can we talk? Outside, not at the desks.'
'If it's about the printer, I've said sorry.'
Lalremsiami kept her voice level. 'It's not only the printer. Last week you threw the stapler. On Monday you shouted in Rina's face until she cried. She asked me whether she could move floors.'
'Everyone here makes me angry. The deadlines are insane.'
'The deadlines are insane for all of us. But I'm seeing this almost every week, and people are scared of you. That's not a bad mood any more.'
Zubin stared at the car park. 'I don't even remember deciding to throw things.'
'I've told our manager so Rina can sit with another team for now. And the company has a counsellor. I think you should see them this week.'
A long silence. 'Will you send me the number?'
'Sending it now.'

qa.q: What did Zubin throw last week?
qa.a: The stapler.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she spoke to Zubin?
qa.a: She was worried and uneasy, seeing a pattern that frightened colleagues, but she stayed steady and level.

qa.q: Which step came first, and why does that order matter?
qa.a: She made sure Rina was safe by telling the manager, then urged Zubin to see a counsellor, because people's safety must come before fixing the pattern.

qa.q: How might Rina have been affected by Zubin's outbursts?
qa.a: She was frightened enough to cry and ask to move floors, so work had stopped feeling safe.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees frequent explosions and intimidation, recognises it as more than a bad mood, puts safety first and points the person to a counsellor.

passage: The first time Charu threw her phone, I laughed it off. We'd shared the flat for a year, and she'd always had a temper. Then it was the bathroom door, slammed so hard the frame cracked. Then a steel plate hurled at the wall, a foot from my head, because I'd used her milk. Each time she apologised the next morning, cheerful again. I started tiptoeing around my own home and checking her mood before I spoke. One night, lying awake with my heart racing, I finally admitted it: this wasn't a bad mood. It was a pattern, and I was scared. The next evening I slept at a friend's place. Then I met Charu at a café and told her, calmly, that I couldn't live with it and that she needed to see a counsellor. She cried. A week later she showed me her appointment card. I'm Ishita, and I'm still learning to trust that flat again.

qa.q: What did Charu throw at the wall?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel living with Charu before that night?
qa.a: Ishita felt scared and on edge, tiptoeing around the flat and checking Charu's mood before speaking.

qa.q: What made Ishita's response sensible?
qa.a: Ishita put personal safety first by staying at a friend's place, then spoke calmly in a public place and pushed for a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Ishita spoke to her at the café?
qa.a: Charu was probably ashamed and upset, which may have helped her take the step of booking an appointment.

grounding: Shows a flatmate who sees repeated explosions and damage, realises it is more than a bad mood, puts safety first and urges counselling.

passage:
Football club note, Saturday
Today, for the third match running, our assistant coach Suraj lost his temper with the under-twelves. After a missed pass he kicked the water crate across the bench and shouted into Aarush's face from very close. Aarush went pale and two other children started crying. I stopped the session, moved the children to the far goal with the second coach, and asked Suraj to leave the ground for the day. Before home time I reported it to the club's welfare officer, who phoned Aarush's parents that evening and met me and Suraj the next morning. Suraj told us he doesn't know why it keeps happening, and that it scares him too. He has agreed to see a counsellor and will not coach until he has. The children will get a calm debrief at Tuesday's practice.
Tanuja, head coach

passage:
Daycare note, Monday
Anand tripped on the mat and bumped his knee. At first no sound came. He gulped air, hiccuped twice, and held his breath, his face going pink. Then the sob burst out. I picked him up and held him against my chest, one hand on his back. I breathed slowly and deeply, in and out, not saying much. After a minute his hiccups slowed and his breathing began to match mine. He rested his head on my shoulder and sniffed.
Jyoti, toddler room

'Now blow out the diya, gently.' He puffed, and the flame wobbled. They did it again and again, giggling. Every night that week they played. On Sunday at the fair, Gautam lost his balloon and started to howl. Seema knelt. 'Where's your jasmine?' Gautam sniffed his fingers, then blew. Smell, blow. His howls slowed to sniffles.

passage: In the kindergarten circle in Margao, Maria Teacher held up a paper flower and a paper candle. 'First we smell the flower, slow and long. Then we blow out the candle, soft and slow.' passage: Thabo came into the Johannesburg kitchen to find his sister Vera riding his new bike round the yard. 'That's MINE!' His chest was heaving. His breath came fast and short, like he'd been running, though he hadn't. He was about to yank her off. Then he remembered what the swimming coach said about breath and nerves. He noticed it: fast, high, tight. He stopped at the door and breathed out long, like blowing a candle out slowly. Once. Twice. Five times. His chest softened. His fists opened. 'Vera. Can you give it back, please? I haven't even ridden it yet.' She rolled her eyes but got off. Thabo felt oddly proud. He had steered his own body, like steering a bike.

qa.q: Who was riding Thabo's new bike?
qa.a: His sister Vera.

qa.a: He was angry, with his breath coming fast and short and his chest heaving.

qa.q: How might Vera have reacted if Thabo had yanked her off?

grounding: Shows a child noticing fast, shallow breath when angry and slowing it, gaining a sense of control over his body.

passage: At the inter-school spelling bee in the auditorium, Minakshi waited in the row of chairs on stage. Her breath was coming in quick little gasps high in her chest. Her hands were cold. Hrithik Sir, the teacher in charge, bent down beside her chair. 'Notice your breathing?' Minakshi nodded. 'Quick.' 'Try this. Breathe in through your nose for three, out through your mouth for five.' She did it three times. Her shoulders dropped. The quick gasps slowed into longer breaths. When her name was called, she walked to the mic. Her voice wobbled on the first word, then steadied. 'Rhythm. R-H-Y-T-H-M.' Back in her chair, she thought, I did that. I made my body calm down.

passage: Jasleen read the message from her best friend three times, then started crying so hard she couldn't stop. In the small bedroom of their Chandigarh flat, her breaths came quicker and quicker, gasp after gasp. Her fingers began to tingle. The room swayed. Now she was scared as well as heartbroken. 'Something's wrong with me,' she sobbed. Her older brother Kunal came in and sat beside her. 'Jasleen, you're breathing too fast. That's what's making you dizzy. Breathe out with me, long. Like you're blowing through a straw.' She tried. Out, long. In, small. Out, longer. After a few minutes the tingling faded, and the room held still. She was still sad, but no longer terrified. 'If this keeps happening, we'll tell Mummy and see the doctor,' Kunal said.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when he heard Jasleen sobbing?
qa.a: He was probably worried, but chose to stay calm and practical for his sister.

passage:
'Tejas? Are you in there? The debate starts in five minutes.'
'Farhan, I can't. My hands are tingling. My head's spinning. I think I'm going to pass out.'
'Open the door. I'm here.' The bolt clicked. Tejas was gulping air by the washbasin.
'You're breathing really fast, bro. That's why you're dizzy. Try breathing out slowly. Longer than in.'
'I can't slow it.'
'Just follow me. Out… two… three… four… five. Small breath in. Out again, long.'
Tejas copied. Once. Twice. Five times.
'Tingling any better?'
'A bit. My head's clearer.'
'Good. Let's tell Ma'am you need a few minutes. If it happens again, tell her or your parents.'
Tejas nodded. 'Thanks, Farhan.'

passage: The night after Nana's funeral, I cried harder than I'd ever cried in my life. Sitting on the terrace, I couldn't catch my breath. I was gulping and gulping, and then my lips went numb and my hands started tingling. I thought, I'm dying too. That made it so much worse. My cousin Nilesh found me there. He didn't panic. He sat close and said, 'Zubin, you're breathing too fast. Your body's getting too much air. Breathe out with me, really slowly.' He breathed out long and loud, like a sigh, and I copied him. After a few minutes the tingling faded. I was still crying, but I wasn't scared any more. Later that night Nilesh told my mother, and she sat with me until I slept. I still think of that terrace when grief hits hard.

qa.q: Where was Zubin sitting when it began?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when the lips went numb?
qa.a: Zubin felt terrified, thinking of dying too, on top of the grief.

qa.a: Nilesh stayed calm, explained the fast breathing and breathed out slowly with Zubin, then told an adult that night.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother have felt when Nilesh told her?
qa.a: She was probably worried and sad, and wanted to stay close so Zubin would not be alone that night.

grounding: Shows a teenager crying hard in grief who over-breathes, feels numb and tingly, grows more afraid, and is calmed by a longer out-breath.

passage:
Friday, 10 pm
Moot court round today. I had the opening submission. When the judge nodded at me, my heart was racing and my shoulders were practically touching my ears. Before, I'd have launched straight in and gabbled. Today I did what I'd practised in the washroom mirror: one long breath out, shoulders down, a second of silence before speaking. It felt like forever, but Pallavi said later it looked like I was simply gathering my notes. My first sentence came out steady, and my thinking stayed clear even when the judge interrupted. Nobody noticed the breath. That's the point. I'm doing it again next round.
Mohit

passage: Nandini, you know how I was always wiped out by five? It's Sarika here, and I finally figured out why. Month-end closing week, I'm doing the accounts, and a colleague walks past and says, 'Sarika, you're holding your breath.' I laughed. Then I caught myself doing it ten minutes later. Just not breathing. Shoulders up by my ears, breathing tiny little sips from the top of my chest. No wonder my neck ached and I felt like a rag by evening. So now I have a sticky note on the monitor that says breathe. When I see it, I take three slow breaths into my belly and drop my shoulders. Takes twenty seconds. I'm not saying it fixes month-end. But I'm not a rag at five any more.

passage: Damini, beta, you look exactly like I did at your age, all hunched over that laptop. Let your Uday Mama tell you something. My first job was at a bank in Pune. Month-end, the ledgers had to balance, and I would sit for hours without moving. I thought I was working hard. Really, I was barely breathing. My chest was tight, my jaw was clenched, and I went home so exhausted I snapped at everyone. One day the old head cashier, Mr Kulkarni, tapped my shoulder. 'Uday, you're holding your breath like a diver. Breathe, man.' He showed me: three slow breaths, deep into the stomach, every time I finished a page. I thought it was silly. But within a week, I stopped going home so tired.

passage:
'Mummy, can I go to the park? Riya's there.'

Charu watched her. 'Ayesha, last Sunday after cricket, you did all your maths in twenty minutes, remember?'

Ayesha raced out. She came back pink-cheeked and calm, sat down and finished her homework without a single complaint.

passage: The monsoon that year lasted forever. For two weeks the colony ground in Kochi was a lake, and my little sister Pooja and I were stuck inside. By the fourth day we were fighting about everything: the TV, the window seat, who breathed too loud. I couldn't fall asleep at night, and my homework took hours. Umma kept saying, 'What's wrong with you two?' Then the rain stopped on a Saturday. We ran out into the mud, played catch till our arms ached, raced each other round the building six times. That night I slept like a stone. On Monday I did my sums in half the time. Pooja and I didn't fight once. I'm Afreen, and I still remember thinking: oh, my body needed that.

qa.q: Where did Afreen and Pooja play when the rain stopped?
qa.a: Out in the mud, round the building.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel during the two weeks stuck inside?
qa.a: Afreen felt restless and irritable, fighting with Pooja and unable to sleep well.

qa.q: What does Afreen's story suggest parents could plan on rainy days?
qa.a: Finding ways for children to move and play, since being stuck indoors made both children cranky and restless.

qa.q: How might Umma have seen the change after the rain stopped?
qa.a: Umma was probably relieved to see the two children calm, sleeping and not fighting.

grounding: Shows a child who argues more and sleeps badly when kept indoors, and whose mood and sleep improve after running and playing outside.

passage:
PE department note to Class 5 teachers
For three weeks Chaitanya has been kept in during PE to finish unfinished classwork. I've noticed that on those days he is more restless, not less. He fidgets in the corridor, argues with classmates and, according to his mother, sleeps badly. On Thursday, by mistake, he came out and played football for the full period. Afterwards Vikas Sir from Class 5B told me Chaitanya finished his English worksheet quietly and even helped tidy up. I'd like to request that PE not be used as a punishment for any child. Running and play help children settle; taking them away seems to make things worse. Happy to discuss other consequences.
Mr Joseph, PE teacher

qa.q: How long has Chaitanya been kept in during PE?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya be feeling on days he misses PE?
qa.a: He seems restless and cranky, fidgeting and arguing with classmates.

qa.q: What did Mr Joseph suggest instead of keeping children in?
qa.a: That PE should not be used as punishment, and that other consequences be discussed.

qa.q: How did Vikas Sir see Chaitanya after the football period?
qa.a: Vikas Sir saw a calmer boy who finished his worksheet quietly and helped tidy up.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a child kept from play is more restless and sleeps worse, and arguing that physical play is part of how children regulate feelings.

passage: The state kabaddi trials were on Sunday, and the heat in Madurai had closed the school ground all week. Keerthana's team practised at six in the morning on the temple lawn instead, with the coach, Hrithik Sir, shouting timings. She loved these girls. Since joining the team in Class 9, she'd stopped dreading school; the laughter, the bruises, the early-morning chai had given her days a shape. But this week felt different. Hrithik Sir kept saying, 'Lose on Sunday and forget the state team.' One of the seniors said Keerthana looked too soft to be selected. At night her mind raced. On Friday, after practice, her friend Anu found her crying behind the lawn. 'I used to love this,' Keerthana said. 'Now it's just more pressure.' Anu sat beside her. 'Then let's remember why we started. Chai first.'

qa.q: Where did the team practise that week?
qa.a: On the temple lawn.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling behind the lawn on Friday?
qa.a: She was stressed and sad, feeling that the sport she loved had become just more pressure.

qa.q: What small step did Anu suggest?
qa.a: Sitting together over chai and remembering why they started playing.

qa.q: How might Hrithik Sir's words affect the other girls?
qa.a: They might also feel anxious and pushed, turning practice into worry instead of fun.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose team sport gives her friends, structure and calm, until pressure to win and comments about her looks turn it into stress.

passage: Evening basketball in the Hyderabad colony court had become the best part of Irfan's day. Since he'd joined the older boys in Class 10, he'd stopped spending evenings alone on his phone, and exam worry felt smaller after two hours of running. He had friends who saved him a spot. Then one of them started joking about his thin arms. 'Stick boy.' The others laughed. Irfan began doing push-ups late at night in his room, and checking his arms in the mirror before every game. Basketball stopped being fun. His elder sister Pooja found him doing push-ups at midnight. 'You're exhausted, Irfan. Why?' He told her. Pooja sat on the bed. 'You loved that court because of the game and your friends, not your arms. Want me to come watch tomorrow?'

qa.q: What did one friend call Irfan?
qa.a: Stick boy.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after the jokes about his arms?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and anxious about his body, and basketball stopped being fun.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that could help Irfan?
qa.a: She asked gently, listened and reminded him why he loved the court, offering to come and watch.

qa.q: How might the friend who joked see the push-ups if Irfan told him?
qa.a: He might be surprised and sorry, not realising a joke had caused so much worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose sport gives him energy, friends and calm about school, until pressure to look a certain way turns it into stress.

passage:
'Good swim today, Chandrika.'
'Thanks, Imran. It was, actually. I felt light.'
'You always look happier after training.'
'I am. Before I joined the club, I was so tense about school. Now I have you lot, and Tuesday pizza, and I actually sleep.'
'So why did you look like you'd seen a ghost when your dad came in?'
Chandrika pulled her towel tighter. 'He's already talking about the national meet. He wrote my times on the fridge. If I don't drop a second by March, he says I'm wasting his time.'
'That sounds like a lot.'
'Some days I love it. Some days the water feels like an exam hall.'
Imran nodded. 'Maybe tell Coach? She's good at talking to parents.'
'Maybe.' She smiled faintly. 'Pizza first.'

qa.q: What does Chandrika's father write on the fridge?
qa.a: Her times.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her father came in?
qa.a: She was anxious and pressured, as if she had seen a ghost.

qa.q: What step did Imran suggest?
qa.a: Telling the coach, who is good at talking to parents.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's father see his pushing?
qa.a: He may believe he is helping her succeed, not seeing how it turns the water into an exam hall for her.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose sport gives her friends, energy and calm about school, while a parent's pressure to win makes it another source of stress.

passage: I'm Suraj, Payal's father, and I'll tell you what I saw last Sunday, though I can't say for sure what was going on inside her. She'd been at her desk since breakfast, online class, then homework, then her phone. By four, she was snapping at everyone. Her mother asked about lunch and got a sharp 'I don't care!' The door banged. I didn't lecture. I knocked and said, 'I'm going to cycle to the lake to buy corn. Want to come? You can ride ahead.' She shrugged, but came. For the first ten minutes she didn't say a word. Then, by the lake, she laughed at a dog chasing ducks. On the way back she told me about a friend's joke. I don't know if it was the air, the cycling or just not being told off. But she was different.

qa.q: What did Suraj go to the lake to buy?
qa.a: Corn.

qa.q: What might Suraj have been feeling when he chose not to lecture?
qa.a: Suraj seems calm and caring, wanting to help rather than scold, even without knowing what was wrong.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Payal on a ride as company, not an order, gave her movement and space without pressure to talk.

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced the ride?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved to get out of the room without being told off, and slowly lighter as she moved.

grounding: Shows, through a parent's account, a teenager snappy after hours at a desk and phone, and a cycling invitation offered as company that lifts her mood.

passage:
Friday: After six hours of online classes and gaming, Nitin snapped at Amandeep over nothing and slammed his laptop shut. Amandeep, his mother, shouted back and he stormed off.
Saturday: He was hunched at the desk again by noon. 'Go out for a walk, you've been sitting all day!' she ordered. 'Stop telling me what to do!' he yelled. It was worse.
Sunday: Amandeep tried something different. She picked up the shopping bag. 'I'm walking to the vegetable market. Come keep me company?' Nitin grumbled but came. They walked twenty minutes, mostly silent. On the way back, he offered to carry the bag and started talking about a new game. At home he was calm all evening.

qa.q: How many hours of online classes and gaming had Nitin done on Friday?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she tried something different on Sunday?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated after two bad days but hopeful that a gentler invitation might work.

qa.q: What was the difference between Saturday and Sunday?
qa.a: On Saturday the walk was an order and made things worse; on Sunday it was an invitation for company, and it helped.

qa.q: How might Nitin have experienced his mother's Sunday invitation?
qa.a: He probably felt less controlled and more wanted, which made it easier to join and relax.

grounding: Shows a parent who sees a teenager snappy after long sitting and learns that movement works better when offered as company, not as an order.

passage: Kiran, you're sighing like the whole world is against you. Let your Sachin Dada tell you something about your Papa. When he was sixteen, before his board exams, he sat at that same desk from morning till night. By evening he'd bite anyone's head off. Your Dadi would scold, and he'd shout, and the whole house would be on fire. I had no clever words. So one evening I just wheeled out my old cycle and said, 'I'm going to the lake. Coming?' He grumbled but came. We didn't talk much. We cycled round the lake twice, watched the boats, and came back. He was a different boy. After that, every evening we cycled. No lectures, just company. He passed, and he still calls those rides the best part of that year.

qa.q: Where did Sachin and his son cycle?
qa.a: Round the lake.

qa.q: How did Kiran's Papa feel after long days at the desk?
qa.a: He was irritable and snappy, biting anyone's head off.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sachin's story?
qa.a: Sachin stopped scolding and simply invited his son on a cycle ride as company.

qa.q: How might Kiran's Dadi have seen the evening rides?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved that the house was calmer and the shouting had stopped.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a parent who notices a teenager snappy after long hours studying and offers cycling as company, which lifts his mood.
